_comment: Sprint 35 curated fishing-guidance catalogue: common surf/pier targets only, region-gated by conditions_region. Every field except id/name/regions is copied verbatim from the legacy storage/species_data.json entry named in legacy_name (provisional dataset, see docs/CANONICAL_ROADMAP.md). Generated by scripts/generate_guidance_catalogue.py; regenerate rather than hand-edit.

species.name: Red drum
species.bait: Cut menhaden or mullet strips; fresh shrimp; live finger mullet when available
species.rig: Fish finder rig with sliding egg sinker
species.lures: Gold/copper spoons, paddle-tail swimbaits (3-5"), Z-Man soft plastics on 1/4-3/8 oz jighead, topwater plugs at dawn/dusk
species.explanation_cold: Winter red drum congregate in deeper marsh channels and holes, foraging along the bottom for shrimp, crabs and small fish.
species.explanation_warm: Red drum actively feed in the surf zone and around inlets, chasing mullet, menhaden and crabs in warmer water.

species.name: Black drum
species.bait: Cut shrimp, clams, blood worms, cut mullet, menhaden or crab pieces
species.rig: Hi-lo rig or fish finder rig
species.lures: Not a primary lure target; slow-rolled paddle-tail swimbaits near oyster structure occasionally work
species.explanation_cold: Black drum are bottom feeders that locate prey with chin barbels; they prefer mollusks, shrimp and crab pieces in cooler water.
species.explanation_warm: Black drum move through inlets and along structure, actively rooting for crabs, clams and shrimp in warming water.

species.name: Bluefish
species.bait: Cut menhaden or mullet; small fish pieces
species.rig: Fish finder rig with steel leader
species.lures: Metal spoons (Hopkins, Kastmaster), topwater poppers, Clarkspoons, metal jigs; bluefish hit almost any fast-moving lure
species.explanation_cold: Smaller bluefish (snappers/tailors) roam nearshore waters and readily hit cut bait; wire or heavy leaders are essential.
species.explanation_warm: Bluefish schools are actively chasing baitfish along the surf line and around piers; cut menhaden and mullet draw explosive strikes.

species.name: Speckled trout
species.bait: Live shrimp (most productive); finger mullet; small menhaden
species.rig: Popping-cork or fishfinder rig on light leader
species.lures: MirrOlure (MR17, 52M), soft plastic tails (Gulp shrimp, DOA Terror Eyz) on 1/4 oz jighead, topwater walk-the-dog lures
species.explanation_cold: Speckled trout hold in deeper holes and backwater creeks; live shrimp or finger mullet entice sluggish winter fish.
species.explanation_warm: Speckled trout are aggressively feeding on shrimp and small baitfish in the shallows and around grass flats.

species.name: Whiting (sea mullet)
species.bait: Fresh shrimp, mole crabs (sand fleas), bloodworms, squid
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs (1/16-1/8 oz) tipped with Fishbites; not a primary lure target
species.explanation_cold: Whiting patrol sandy bottoms along beaches and piers; they feed on shrimp, mole crabs and worms in the winter surf.
species.explanation_warm: Whiting are schooling up along the beach and biting aggressively on shrimp and sand fleas in the wash zone.

species.name: Spot
species.bait: Bloodworms; small pieces of shrimp; Fishbites
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Rarely taken on lures; not a primary lure target
species.explanation_cold: Spot are mostly offshore or in deeper channels during winter; occasional catches from piers on warmer days.
species.explanation_warm: Spot are schooling along the beach and around piers, biting aggressively on bloodworms and shrimp pieces.

species.name: Atlantic croaker
species.bait: Fresh shrimp pieces; bloodworms; squid strips; Fishbites
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Not typically lure-caught; small jigs occasionally work
species.explanation_cold: Croaker move to deeper channels and offshore in winter; occasional catches from piers on mild days.
species.explanation_warm: Croaker are schooling along the surf and around piers, making their signature croaking sound; they hit shrimp and worms aggressively.

species.name: Sheepshead
species.bait: Live fiddler crabs; sand fleas; small pieces of shrimp
species.rig: Knocker rig with short fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Rarely taken on lures; small jigs with soft crab imitations near pilings occasionally work
species.explanation_cold: Sheepshead feed around pilings and rock structures, nibbling barnacles and crustaceans; bites are subtle and require fishing straight down.
species.explanation_warm: Sheepshead stack up around nearshore structure and pilings, picking at barnacles and crabs before moving offshore for spawning.

species.name: Flounder
species.bait: Live finger mullet; live minnows; fresh shrimp under a bucktail jig
species.rig: Fish finder rig with 24-36 in fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Bucktail jig (1/4-1/2 oz) with paddle tail, Gulp Nemesis or shrimp, Carolina-rigged swimming grub bounced on bottom
species.explanation_cold: Flounder are mostly offshore in cold water; stragglers around inlets may bite live mullet drifted slowly along the bottom.
species.explanation_warm: Flounder are ambushing baitfish in the surf, around inlets and near pier pilings; live finger mullet is the top producer.

species.name: Pompano
species.bait: Sand fleas (mole crabs); fresh shrimp; Fishbites
species.rig: Pompano rig with float beads above hooks
species.lures: Pompano jigs (1/4-3/8 oz, yellow/orange/chartreuse), Silly Willy jigs, Clouser minnows near breaking waves
species.explanation_cold: Pompano are scarce inshore during cold months; occasional catches occur on warmer days near the surf zone.
species.explanation_warm: Pompano are running the surf line feeding on sand fleas and small crustaceans; target the troughs and holes along the beach.

species.name: Spanish mackerel
species.bait: Shiny spoons; live baitfish; small plugs; fresh shrimp on a long-shank hook
species.rig: Float rig with wire leader, free-lined or under float
species.lures: Clarkspoon (1/0-3/0) on inline spinner or planer, small metal jigs, silver or gold spoons; fast retrieve
species.explanation_cold: Spanish mackerel have migrated south; they are not present in nearshore NC waters during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Spanish mackerel are blitzing baitfish just behind the breakers and around piers; they hit flashy spoons and small baits.

species.name: Snook
species.bait: Live mullet; live shrimp; live menhaden; topwater plugs
species.rig: Fish finder rig with heavy fluorocarbon leader or free-lined
species.lures: Large soft plastic jerkbaits, DOA Baitbuster, topwater walk-the-dog plugs, Rapala X-Rap; target structure and inlet edges
species.explanation_cold: Snook are a tropical species not found in NC during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Snook are rare visitors to NC during unusually warm summers; they are prized gamefish that ambush bait around inlets, docks and structure.

species.name: Striped bass
species.bait: Cut menhaden, mullet or shad; live mullet or eels
species.rig: Fish finder rig with heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Bucktail jigs (1-3 oz), soft plastic swimbaits, topwater plugs (Rapala X-Rap, Bomber), metal jigs at night under lights
species.explanation_cold: Striped bass are found around piers, jetties and surf troughs; winter surf anglers use cut or live bait on heavy tackle.
species.explanation_warm: Striped bass push through inlets chasing schools of mullet and menhaden; they are most active at dawn and dusk.

species.name: Tautog
species.bait: Pieces of fresh shrimp, sand fleas, fiddler or rock crabs, clams
species.rig: Knocker rig with heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Not a strong lure target; slow-rolled swimbaits near rocky structure occasionally work
species.explanation_cold: Tautog cling to jetties and rock piles in winter, feeding on crustaceans; they require strong tackle and small, strong hooks.
species.explanation_warm: Tautog become less active as water warms and move to deeper structure; early spring offers a window before they thin out.

species.name: Black sea bass
species.bait: Strips of squid or cut fish; shrimp
species.rig: Hi-lo rig on braided line
species.lures: Small jigs (1-2 oz bucktail), soft plastic crabs/shrimp on drop-shot rigs, small diamond jigs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Inshore black sea bass inhabit wrecks and hard bottom, feeding on crabs, shrimp and small fish; bottom-fish with squid or cut bait.
species.explanation_warm: Black sea bass are abundant over nearshore reefs and wrecks, aggressively hitting squid strips and cut bait.

species.name: Barred surfperch
species.bait: Sand crabs (mole crabs); bloodworms; Gulp! sandworms; small pieces of mussel
species.rig: Carolina rig with light leader; sliding sinker rig
species.lures: Small paddle-tail swimbaits (2-3"), Berkley Gulp Sand Crab, tube jigs in the surf zone
species.explanation_cold: Barred surfperch are actively spawning and feeding aggressively in the winter surf zone -- this is peak season on the Pacific Coast.
species.explanation_warm: Barred surfperch are present but less concentrated; they move to deeper water as surf warms.

species.name: Redtail surfperch
species.bait: Sand crabs; sand shrimp; pile worms; Gulp! sandworms
species.rig: Carolina rig or double dropper loop rig
species.lures: Small paddle tails, Gulp Sand Crab in the surf; same tactics as barred surfperch
species.explanation_cold: Redtail surfperch school up in the surf zone during winter and early spring, feeding heavily on sand crabs in the wash.
species.explanation_warm: Redtail surfperch are less common in the surf during warmer months; try rocky areas and jetties.

species.name: California halibut
species.bait: Live anchovy; live smelt; squid strips; Gulp! grubs; swim baits
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig with fluorocarbon leader; Carolina rig; jig head
species.sinker: 1-3 oz sliding egg or banana sinker
species.lures: Live bait-style swimbaits, paddle tails on 3/8-3/4 oz jighead, Berkley Gulp grubs drifted on bottom
species.explanation_cold: California halibut are in deeper water during cold months and less accessible from shore.
species.explanation_warm: California halibut move into shallow sandy areas near piers, jetties, and in the surf zone to ambush baitfish; cast parallel to shore and retrieve slowly along the bottom.

species.name: Corbina
species.bait: Sand crabs; bloodworms; mussels; clam
species.rig: Carolina rig with light fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Berkley Gulp Sand Crab, small swimbaits, Yamamoto Senko-style worms in the surf
species.explanation_cold: Corbina move to deeper water and are hard to reach from shore in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Corbina cruise the SoCal surf zone rooting for sand crabs and worms in the wash; they are the prized surf species of Southern California.

species.name: Yellowfin croaker
species.bait: Sand crabs; mussels; bloodworms; cut squid
species.rig: Carolina rig; sliding sinker rig
species.lures: Small swimbaits, Gulp lures
species.explanation_cold: Yellowfin croaker are deeper and less active during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Yellowfin croaker are common in the SoCal and central CA surf zone; they school up and feed aggressively on sand crabs.

species.name: Black rockfish
species.bait: Live or cut herring; tube worms; squid strips; live anchovies
species.rig: Light to medium tackle; drift-fishing with a single hook on 20-30 lb leader; jig straight down to schools
species.lures: Tube jigs in black/purple, soft plastic paddle tails, metal jigs (Crippled Herring), and Buzz Bombs — black rockfish readily hit surface lures
species.explanation_cold: Black rockfish hold near rocky reefs and kelp at 30-150 ft year-round; they are less active in winter but can be found schooling tight to structure.
species.explanation_warm: Spring and summer are prime for black rockfish along the Pacific coast; they school near the surface around kelp beds and rocky points and aggressively hit surface poppers, tube jigs, and cut herring.

species.name: Lingcod
species.bait: Live bait (smelt, anchovy); large swimbaits; jigs tipped with squid
species.rig: Heavy jig head or dropper loop rig with large swimbait
species.lures: Large swimbaits (5-8"), heavy jigs (4-8 oz), plastic eels; very aggressive; retrieve with erratic action
species.explanation_cold: Lingcod move into shallower rocky reefs during fall and winter to spawn; they are aggressive ambush predators accessible from jetties and rocky points.
species.explanation_warm: Lingcod retreat to deeper water offshore during warm months; less accessible from shore.

species.name: Ulua (giant trevally)
species.bait: Live akule (bigeye scad); live opelu; large cut bait; whole octopus
species.rig: Heavy sliding sinker rig with 100+ lb leader; ulua setup
species.lures: Large poppers, stickbaits (GT poppers), heavy swimbaits; very powerful fighter
species.explanation_cold: Giant trevally are present year-round in Hawaii but slightly less active during cooler months.
species.explanation_warm: Giant trevally (ulua) are the ultimate shore-fishing trophy in Hawaii; they're powerful predators caught from rocky shores and piers on heavy tackle.

species.name: Papio
species.bait: Live opelu; cut squid; shrimp; small crabs; poppers
species.rig: Light papio rig; float rig; small sliding sinker
species.lures: Small jigs, spoons, swimbaits; juvenile jacks are aggressive
species.explanation_cold: Papio are present year-round in Hawaii; smaller jacks are always near shore.
species.explanation_warm: Papio are the most popular shore-fishing target in Hawaii; these juvenile jacks roam reefs and harbors and are a great family fishing species.

species.name: O'io (bonefish)
species.bait: Shrimp; sand crabs; small crabs; squid strips; fly fishing (Christmas Island specials)
species.rig: Light Carolina rig with fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Clouser minnows, shrimp fly imitations, Crazy Charlie flies; almost exclusively sight-fished with lures/flies
species.explanation_cold: Bonefish are present year-round in Hawaii flats but slightly less active in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Bonefish (oio) feed on shallow sand flats in Hawaii; they are the ghosts of the flats -- fast, wary, and an incredible fight on light tackle.

species.name: Moi
species.bait: Sand crabs; shrimp; cut squid; small crabs
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig in the surf; Carolina rig with fluorocarbon
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics; delicate fighters
species.explanation_cold: Moi are present in cooler months but less concentrated in the shallows.
species.explanation_warm: Moi (Pacific threadfin) is Hawaii's most revered eating fish; once reserved for royalty, they feed in the sandy surf zone and are caught from beaches and piers.

species.name: Weakfish (gray trout)
species.bait: Live shrimp; small live mullet; cut bait strips
species.rig: Fish finder rig with light fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Paddle-tail soft plastics on 1/4 oz jighead, metal spoons, shrimp imitations
species.explanation_cold: Gray trout hold in deeper holes near inlets; they feed slowly and prefer live shrimp drifted near the bottom.
species.explanation_warm: Gray trout are feeding actively around inlets and along the beach, hitting live shrimp and small baitfish near structure.

species.name: Scup (porgy)
species.bait: Squid strips; shrimp pieces; clam; bloodworms
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs, sabiki rigs; not a primary lure target
species.explanation_cold: Scup migrate nearshore during fall and winter, schooling over structure and hard bottom.
species.explanation_warm: Scup are transitioning to and from offshore; spring and fall offer the best nearshore action over reefs and wrecks.

species.name: Winter flounder
species.bait: Sandworms; bloodworms; clam strips; mussel
species.rig: Spreader rig or hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs, Gulp grubs; primarily bait caught but jigs work in clean water
species.explanation_cold: Winter flounder move inshore to bays and harbors in late winter to spawn; they are a cold-water staple of Northeast pier and jetty anglers.
species.explanation_warm: Winter flounder move offshore as water warms past 60°F; they are rarely caught from shore in summer.

species.name: Atlantic mackerel
species.bait: Sabiki rigs (best); small pieces of clam, squid, or any shiny flash
species.rig: Sabiki rig with 6-8 size 8-10 hooks; drift in the current over schools
species.sinker: 1-4 oz to get rig to depth
species.lures: Tiny metal jigs (1/4-1/2 oz), small spoons, Sabiki rigs
species.explanation_cold: Atlantic mackerel overwinter offshore in deep water; they return to coastal waters in spring as the biggest schools of the year push north.
species.explanation_warm: Mackerel are a schooling species accessible from piers, jetties, and boats spring through early summer; they are one of the best live baits for stripers, blues, and tuna — and excellent eating.

species.name: False albacore
species.bait: Live sand eels, small herring, bay anchovies; crash surface bait schools
species.rig: Light to medium spinning with small lures; 15-20 lb leader ideal
species.lures: Hogy Epoxy jigs, small metal spoons, sand eel fly patterns; match the hatch exactly
species.explanation_cold: Little tunny are fall visitors along the entire East Coast from Maine to Florida; the fall run can be spectacular.
species.explanation_warm: September through November is 'albie season' — they crash bait schools along the coast and are one of the fastest and most exciting fish on light tackle.

species.name: Atlantic bonito
species.bait: Small metal jigs; live small baitfish; trolling feathers; cut bait strips
species.rig: Float rig with fluorocarbon leader or casting jig
species.lures: Small metal jigs, spoons, feather jigs; fast retrieve through busting fish
species.explanation_cold: Atlantic bonito pass through NC waters during fall and spring migrations and may be present in cooler months.
species.explanation_warm: Atlantic bonito school nearshore and around piers during migration; they are fast, aggressive fish that hit small jigs and live baits.

species.name: Northern kingfish
species.bait: Bloodworms; fresh shrimp; sand fleas; Fishbites
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs; not a primary lure target
species.explanation_cold: Northern kingfish (the true 'whiting') are in deeper water during the coldest months but accessible in mild winters.
species.explanation_warm: Northern kingfish are the classic NC whiting, common in the surf during spring and fall; they prefer cooler water than their southern and gulf cousins.

species.name: Cunner (bergall)
species.bait: Small shrimp pieces; clam; bloodworms; sandworms
species.rig: Knocker rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Cunner are small wrasse-like fish that cling to structure year-round; they are one of the few species that consistently bite in cold water.
species.explanation_warm: Cunner become less active in warmer water and are replaced by other structure species.

species.name: Pollock
species.bait: Cut squid; clam; shrimp; jigs; cut fish
species.rig: Hi-lo rig or jig
species.lures: Metal jigs, swimbaits, diamond jigs; excellent jig target in cold water
species.explanation_cold: Pollock are rare visitors to NC waters during exceptionally cold winters; they are more common further north but occasionally appear.
species.explanation_warm: Pollock are a cold-water species not present in NC during warm months.

species.name: White perch
species.bait: Bloodworms; small shrimp; small minnows; tiny jigs
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs, spinners, soft plastics
species.explanation_cold: White perch are in deeper brackish channels during cold months but can be caught on bloodworms.
species.explanation_warm: White perch are found in brackish tidal creeks and the ICW near the coast; they school in good numbers and bite small baits readily.

species.name: Hickory shad
species.bait: Small shad darts; tiny spoons; small jigs tipped with shrimp
species.rig: Tandem shad dart rig
species.lures: Shad darts (1/8-1/4 oz), small spoons, small Clouser minnows in rivers
species.explanation_cold: Hickory shad are staging offshore before their spring spawning run up coastal rivers.
species.explanation_warm: Hickory shad make massive spring runs up NC rivers; they are caught from bridges, piers and banks on small shad darts and jigs.

species.name: American eel
species.bait: Cut fish; shrimp; worms; chicken liver
species.rig: Fish finder rig or double-dropper bottom rig
species.lures: Small soft plastic jigs, worm-style soft baits; occasionally taken on lures
species.explanation_cold: American eels are less active during cold months but can be found in deeper channels and around structure.
species.explanation_warm: American eels are caught around piers, docks and inlets, especially at night; they are slimy and hard to handle but make outstanding live bait for stripers and cobia.

species.name: Northern puffer (blowfish)
species.bait: Small pieces of shrimp, bloodworms or squid
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs with soft plastic; rarely targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: These small, delicious fish are common in late fall and winter; they nibble shrimp and squid pieces on small hooks.
species.explanation_warm: Northern puffers move inshore with warming water, readily biting small pieces of shrimp or squid near structure.

species.name: Sea robin
species.bait: Squid strips; cut shrimp; bloodworms; cut fish
species.rig: Hi-lo rig
species.lures: Small jigs; incidentally caught; not typically targeted
species.explanation_cold: Sea robins are common winter bottom fish around piers and in the surf; they crawl along the bottom using modified pectoral fins.
species.explanation_warm: Sea robins are moving offshore as water warms; occasional catches from piers and the surf in spring and fall.

species.name: Smooth dogfish
species.bait: Cut shrimp; cut fish; squid; clam; any cut bait
species.rig: Fish finder rig with heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Small jigs occasionally; primarily caught on bait
species.explanation_cold: Smooth dogfish are less common inshore during the coldest months but may be present in deeper channels.
species.explanation_warm: Smooth dogfish are one of the most common sharks caught from piers and the surf; they pull hard and eat almost any cut bait on the bottom.

species.name: Spiny dogfish
species.bait: Cut fish; cut squid; shrimp; any oily cut bait
species.rig: Hi-lo rig or Carolina rig
species.lures: Small jigs occasionally; primarily caught on bait
species.explanation_cold: Spiny dogfish are abundant inshore during winter, schooling along the bottom and readily hitting cut bait; handle carefully due to venomous dorsal spines.
species.explanation_warm: Spiny dogfish migrate to cooler northern or deeper waters during warm months and are absent from NC inshore waters.

species.name: Clearnose skate
species.bait: Cut shrimp; cut squid; clam; cut fish; bloodworms
species.rig: Hi-lo rig or Carolina rig
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Clearnose skates are very common bottom catches from piers during winter; they are flat, diamond-shaped rays with translucent nose patches.
species.explanation_warm: Clearnose skates move to deeper, cooler water as temperatures rise and are uncommon inshore during summer.

species.name: Cobia
species.bait: Live eels; live menhaden; large live shrimp
species.rig: Fish finder rig, heavy tackle, or free-lined live bait
species.sinker: 2-4 oz egg sinker or none for free-lining
species.lures: Large paddle-tail swimbaits on 1-3 oz jighead, bucktail jigs, soft plastic eels; sight-fish near rays and manta
species.explanation_cold: Cobia have migrated south and are not present in NC waters during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Cobia are cruising near the surface around piers, buoys and structure; sight-cast live eels or large baits to visible fish.

species.name: King mackerel
species.bait: Live cigar minnows; live menhaden; live blue runners
species.rig: King mackerel stinger rig with wire leader and trailing treble
species.sinker: None or 1 oz egg for slow-trolling
species.lures: Clarkspoons on planers, Drone spoons, dive-bomb rigs; troll at 6-8 knots with stinger hook setup
species.explanation_cold: King mackerel have migrated south and are not available in NC nearshore waters during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Kings are cruising near piers and along the beach chasing baitfish schools; slow-troll or float live baits on wire leader.

species.name: Atlantic spadefish
species.bait: Small pieces of clam; jellyfish pieces; cannonball jellyfish strips
species.rig: Knocker rig with light fluorocarbon leader and small hooks
species.lures: Rarely lure-caught; ultra-light jigs occasionally take them near jellyfish
species.explanation_cold: Spadefish are offshore and unavailable inshore during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Spadefish school around pier pilings and buoys in large numbers; they feed on jellyfish and small invertebrates near the surface.

species.name: Gray triggerfish
species.bait: Small pieces of squid; cut shrimp; sand fleas; fiddler crabs
species.rig: Knocker rig with small strong hooks
species.lures: Small jigs (1-2 oz) with squid strip; not a primary hard-lure target
species.explanation_cold: Triggerfish move to deeper offshore waters in winter and are not available inshore.
species.explanation_warm: Triggerfish stack up around pier pilings, jetties and hard structure; they steal bait expertly so use small, strong hooks.

species.name: Southern flounder
species.bait: Live finger mullet; live minnows; live shrimp; fresh cut mullet strips
species.rig: Fish finder rig with 24-36 in fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Bucktail jigs with paddle tail, Gulp shrimp/Nemesis; same technique as summer flounder
species.explanation_cold: Southern flounder move offshore to spawn in late fall and are scarce inshore during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Southern flounder are the primary flounder species in NC inshore waters; they ambush prey around inlets, docks and creek mouths.

species.name: Gulf flounder
species.bait: Live finger mullet; live shrimp; live minnows; cut mullet strips
species.rig: Fish finder rig with 24-36 in fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Bucktail jigs with paddle tail, Gulp grubs; same as summer flounder
species.explanation_cold: Gulf flounder move offshore during the coldest months; occasional catches near inlets on warmer days.
species.explanation_warm: Gulf flounder are found alongside summer and southern flounder in the surf and around inlets; live finger mullet on the bottom is the top bait.

species.name: Southern kingfish
species.bait: Fresh shrimp; sand fleas; bloodworms; Fishbites
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs (1/16-1/8 oz); not a primary lure target
species.explanation_cold: Southern kingfish are in deeper water during the coldest months but move inshore earlier than northern kingfish.
species.explanation_warm: Southern kingfish (ground mullet) are a whiting species common in the surf; they are slightly larger than northern kingfish and prefer sandy bottom.

species.name: Gulf kingfish
species.bait: Sand fleas; fresh shrimp; Fishbites; bloodworms
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs; not a primary lure target
species.explanation_cold: Gulf kingfish are in deeper water during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Gulf kingfish are the largest whiting species, occasionally exceeding 3 lbs; they prefer high-energy surf zones and hit sand fleas and shrimp.

species.name: Silver perch
species.bait: Small pieces of shrimp; bloodworms; squid bits; Fishbites
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics
species.explanation_cold: Silver perch move to deeper channels during cold months and are uncommon inshore.
species.explanation_warm: Silver perch are common panfish caught from piers and the surf; they school in good numbers and bite small baits readily.

species.name: Sand seatrout (white trout)
species.bait: Live shrimp; small cut fish; squid strips; cut shrimp
species.rig: Fish finder rig with light fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Soft plastic tails on light jighead, small spoons; similar to speckled trout
species.explanation_cold: Sand seatrout move to deeper channels and are less common inshore during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Sand seatrout are smaller cousins of speckled trout, common from piers and in the surf; they school in good numbers and hit shrimp and cut bait.

species.name: Silver seatrout
species.bait: Live shrimp; small cut fish; squid strips; cut shrimp
species.rig: Fish finder rig with light fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastic tails
species.explanation_cold: Silver seatrout are in deeper channels during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Silver seatrout are similar to sand seatrout but with a more silvery sheen; they school around piers and in the surf and hit live shrimp readily.

species.name: Pinfish
species.bait: Small pieces of shrimp; bread balls; squid bits
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with very small hooks
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Pinfish move to deeper water during cold months and are scarce inshore.
species.explanation_warm: Pinfish are everywhere around piers, docks and structure; excellent live bait when caught on sabiki rigs or small hooks.

species.name: Mangrove snapper
species.bait: Live shrimp; small live baitfish; cut shrimp; small crabs
species.rig: Knocker rig with fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastic shrimp/grubs, topwater at night near docks and bridges
species.explanation_cold: Mangrove snapper are in deeper or more southern waters during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Mangrove snapper stack up around pier pilings, docks, jetties and inlets; they are line-shy and require light fluorocarbon leader.

species.name: Jack crevalle
species.bait: Live menhaden; live mullet; large shrimp; topwater plugs
species.rig: Fish finder rig with heavy leader or free-lined live bait
species.lures: Topwater plugs, fast-retrieved metal jigs, poppers; jacks are aggressive and hit almost any fast lure
species.explanation_cold: Jack crevalle move to warmer southern waters during winter months.
species.explanation_warm: Jack crevalle are aggressive predators that crash baitfish schools in the surf, inlets and around piers; they put up a brutal fight on any tackle.

species.name: Blue runner
species.bait: Small jigs; live shrimp; cut bait; sabiki rigs
species.rig: Hi-lo rig or sabiki with light tackle
species.lures: Small metal jigs, spoons; also caught incidentally on sabiki rigs
species.explanation_cold: Blue runners are offshore or have migrated south during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Blue runners school around piers and nearshore structure; they are excellent live bait for king mackerel and great fun on light tackle.

species.name: Ladyfish
species.bait: Small jigs; live shrimp; small cut bait; spoons
species.rig: Float rig or free-lined with light tackle
species.lures: Small metal jigs, spoons, soft plastic tails; acrobatic fighters that hit readily
species.explanation_cold: Ladyfish move to warmer waters during cold months and are absent from NC.
species.explanation_warm: Ladyfish (skipjack) are fast, acrobatic fish that school in inlets and along the surf; they hit small lures and live shrimp aggressively.

species.name: Tarpon
species.bait: Live menhaden; live mullet; large live shrimp
species.rig: Fish finder rig, heavy tackle, or free-lined live bait
species.lures: Large swimbaits (6-9"), topwater plugs, soft plastic eels, DOA Baitbuster; target in passes and inlets
species.explanation_cold: Tarpon are a tropical species not present in NC waters during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Tarpon are cruising near inlets and along the beach; they hit large live baits and put up spectacular aerial fights.

species.name: Tripletail
species.bait: Live shrimp; small live crabs; small live baitfish
species.rig: Fish finder rig with fluorocarbon leader or free-lined
species.lures: Soft plastic crabs, shrimp flies near floating debris
species.explanation_cold: Tripletail are in warmer southern waters during winter months.
species.explanation_warm: Tripletail lay on their sides near buoys, crab pot floats and floating debris; sight-cast live shrimp or small crabs to visible fish.

species.name: Permit
species.bait: Live crabs; sand fleas; live shrimp
species.rig: Fish finder rig with fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Crab imitations (Del Brown Merkin fly, soft plastic crabs), weighted crab lures on the flats; fly fishing staple
species.explanation_cold: Permit are a tropical species not typically found in NC during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Permit occasionally visit NC waters during peak summer; they feed on crabs and crustaceans and are a prized catch when encountered.

species.name: Lookdown
species.bait: Small pieces of shrimp; tiny jigs; sand fleas
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks and light leader
species.lures: Small jigs; incidentally caught
species.explanation_cold: Lookdowns move to warmer waters during cold months and are not present inshore.
species.explanation_warm: Lookdowns school around pier pilings and structure; their flat silver bodies make them unmistakable and they bite small baits near the bottom.

species.name: Great barracuda
species.bait: Live baitfish; flashy spoons or plugs; tube lures
species.rig: Float rig with heavy wire leader
species.lures: Long tube lures, Stretch plugs trolled slowly, large silver spoons; needlefish-style
species.explanation_cold: Barracuda are in warmer tropical waters during winter and rarely found off NC.
species.explanation_warm: Great barracuda occasionally show up around piers and nearshore structure in NC during warm months; they are explosive strikers.

species.name: Bonefish
species.bait: Live shrimp, small crabs near sandy flats
species.rig: Light fly or spinning near tailing bonefish on shallow flats
species.lures: Crazy Charlie, Gotcha, small crab and shrimp flies sight-fished on flats
species.explanation_cold: Bonefish are the iconic flats gamefish of the Florida Keys; catch-and-release only in Florida.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round in Florida Keys flats; sight-fished on shallow sand and marl flats — incredibly fast and powerful for their size. Almost exclusively catch-and-release.

species.name: Sand perch
species.bait: Small pieces of shrimp; squid strips; cut fish; bloodworms
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Sand perch are in deeper water during cold months and seldom caught inshore.
species.explanation_warm: Sand perch are colorful, aggressive little bottom fish found over hard bottom and around structure; they readily hit small cut baits.

species.name: Tomtate
species.bait: Small squid strips; shrimp pieces; cut fish bits
species.rig: Hi-lo rig with small hooks
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near structure
species.explanation_cold: Tomtate grunt move to deeper reefs during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Tomtate are small, abundant grunts that school around pier pilings and nearshore structure; they are reliable biters and useful as live bait.

species.name: Oyster toadfish
species.bait: Cut shrimp; cut fish; squid; crabs
species.rig: Hi-lo rig or Carolina rig
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Toadfish hunker down in structure and are less active during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Oyster toadfish lurk around pier pilings, rocks and oyster beds; they have a painful bite and loud grunting call during spawning season.

species.name: Atlantic sharpnose shark
species.bait: Cut fish; fresh shrimp; squid; any cut bait
species.rig: Fish finder rig with wire leader
species.lures: Primarily caught on bait; small jigs occasionally
species.explanation_cold: Atlantic sharpnose sharks move offshore or south during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Sharpnose sharks are the most common small shark caught from piers and the surf; they readily hit almost any cut bait.

species.name: Sandbar shark
species.bait: Large cut menhaden; cut bluefish; fresh mullet chunks
species.rig: Fish finder rig with wire leader
species.lures: Primarily caught on bait
species.explanation_cold: Sandbar sharks migrate to deeper offshore waters or south during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Sandbar sharks are one of the most abundant large sharks nearshore in NC; target them from piers or the surf with heavy cut bait.

species.name: Blacktip shark
species.bait: Cut menhaden or mullet; fresh bluefish chunks; live bait on heavy tackle
species.rig: Fish finder rig with wire leader
species.lures: Large fast-retrieved swimbaits; primarily caught on bait
species.explanation_cold: Blacktip sharks have migrated south and are not present in NC nearshore waters during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Blacktip sharks are cruising the surf zone and around piers chasing baitfish schools; they are one of the most common sharks caught from shore.

species.name: Spinner shark
species.bait: Cut menhaden; fresh mullet chunks; live bluefish
species.rig: Fish finder rig with wire leader
species.lures: Large fast-retrieved surface lures; primarily caught on bait
species.explanation_cold: Spinner sharks migrate south for winter and are absent from NC waters.
species.explanation_warm: Spinner sharks are feeding in the surf zone, often leaping and spinning out of the water while chasing baitfish.

species.name: Bonnethead shark
species.bait: Live shrimp; cut shrimp; small crabs; cut fish
species.rig: Fish finder rig with light wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Soft plastic crab/shrimp imitations on the flats; primarily bait-caught
species.explanation_cold: Bonnethead sharks migrate south and are not present in NC during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Bonnetheads are the smallest hammerhead species; they cruise grass flats, inlets and the surf feeding on shrimp and crabs.

species.name: Bull shark
species.bait: Large cut menhaden; stingray chunks; live bluefish; bonito heads
species.rig: Shark rig with heavy wire leader
species.lures: Large swimbaits or jigs; primarily caught on bait
species.explanation_cold: Bull sharks move to warmer southern waters during winter months.
species.explanation_warm: Bull sharks patrol inlets, piers and the surf zone; they are powerful fighters requiring very heavy tackle and wire leader.

species.name: Atlantic stingray
species.bait: Cut shrimp; squid; cut fish
species.rig: Fish finder rig
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Atlantic stingrays are in deeper water during cold months and less likely to be encountered.
species.explanation_warm: Atlantic stingrays are the small, very common stingrays that bury in the sand in the surf zone; shuffle your feet to avoid stepping on them.

species.name: Southern stingray
species.bait: Cut shrimp; squid; cut fish; sand fleas
species.rig: Fish finder rig with heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Southern stingrays move to deeper water or migrate south during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Southern stingrays are common in the surf and around piers; they are powerful fighters often caught incidentally while bottom fishing.

species.name: Cownose ray
species.bait: Cut shrimp; clam pieces; crab; cut bait
species.rig: Fish finder rig with heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Cownose rays migrate south in large schools during fall and are absent from NC in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Cownose rays travel in large schools through the surf and inlets; they are strong fighters often hooked while bottom fishing for other species.

species.name: Calico surfperch
species.bait: Sand crabs; bloodworms; small pieces of shrimp
species.rig: Carolina rig with light line
species.lures: Small jigs, Gulp lures in the surf
species.explanation_cold: Calico surfperch are abundant in the Northern California and Oregon surf during winter months.
species.explanation_warm: Calico surfperch move to slightly deeper water but can still be found near jetties.

species.name: Walleye surfperch
species.bait: Pile worms; small shrimp; Gulp! baits; small pieces of mussel
species.rig: Hi-lo rig; float rig; light Carolina rig
species.lures: Small paddle tails, jigs in the surf
species.explanation_cold: Walleye surfperch move to deeper water in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Walleye surfperch are a staple pier catch in California; they school around pilings and rocky areas and are fun on light gear.

species.name: Silver surfperch
species.bait: Pile worms, amphipods, small shrimp in surf and nearshore
species.rig: Ultra-light surf or spinning rig in the surf zone
species.lures: Tiny soft plastic grubs in the surf
species.explanation_cold: Silver surfperch are a small but common surfperch in the surf zone and nearshore Pacific coast.
species.explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Pacific surf and nearshore; silver surfperch run in schools in the surf — fun on ultra-light tackle.

species.name: Rubberlip seaperch
species.bait: Pile worms; mussels; small pieces of shrimp; sand crabs
species.rig: Light Carolina rig; hi-lo rig around structure
species.lures: Small jigs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Rubberlip seaperch hold near rocky structure and pilings during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Rubberlip seaperch feed actively around piers, jetties, and rocky shorelines; they are one of the largest surfperch species.

species.name: Pile perch
species.bait: Mussels, small clams, sandworms, tube worms near pilings and rocky structure
species.rig: Light float or bottom rig at 5-30 ft near dock pilings, rocky jetties, and kelp
species.lures: Small tube jigs, tiny grubs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Pile perch are a schooling species around pilings and jetties year-round; they are less active in coldest winter months.
species.explanation_warm: Spring through fall is peak for pile perch near harbor pilings and rocky structure; one of the most common pier perch in California and good eating when kept fresh.

species.name: Striped seaperch
species.bait: Mussels, tube worms, sandworms, tiny shrimp near exposed rocky coast
species.rig: Light to medium surf rig or float rig near rocky jetties and surge zones
species.lures: Small metal jigs, tube jigs near rocky structure
species.explanation_cold: Striped seaperch favor exposed rocky shorelines and jetties; they are active year-round but most accessible spring through fall.
species.explanation_warm: Spring and summer on rocky exposed coastline at 5-30 ft; one of the deeper-reaching surfperch, sometimes caught to 80 ft near offshore rocky pinnacles.

species.name: Shiner perch
species.bait: Sandworms, tiny clam bits, very small shrimp pieces; tiny baits on tiny hooks
species.rig: Ultra-light float or bottom rig; 4-6 lb line with size 8-12 hooks
species.lures: Micro tube jigs, tiny grubs
species.explanation_cold: Shiner perch are extremely abundant in California bays and estuaries year-round; they are easiest to catch near eelgrass beds.
species.explanation_warm: Spring and summer in eelgrass beds and near pilings; shiner perch are excellent live bait for larger halibut and are great fun for kids on ultra-light gear.

species.name: Black perch
species.bait: Pile worms, shrimp, mussels near rocky reef, pilings, and kelp in bays and nearshore
species.rig: Light rig near rocky reef and dock pilings
species.lures: Small grubs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Black perch (butano perch) are a common surfperch in California rocky areas and around dock pilings; they are darker-colored than other surfperch.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round on California rocky reef and dock pilings; black perch are a versatile surfperch caught anywhere there is rocky structure or pilings — good eating.

species.name: Jacksmelt
species.bait: Small pieces of pile worm; tiny shrimp; Sabiki rigs; small dough balls
species.rig: Multi-hook Sabiki rig or float rig with small hook
species.sinker: Split shot or small torpedo sinker
species.lures: Small jigs, sabiki rigs
species.explanation_cold: Jacksmelt are less concentrated near shore in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Jacksmelt are one of the most common pier fish in California; they school near the surface and are fun on ultra-light tackle.

species.name: White croaker
species.bait: Cut squid; cut anchovy; pile worms; shrimp; almost anything
species.rig: Hi-lo rig; Carolina rig
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics
species.explanation_cold: White croaker are deeper during winter months.
species.explanation_warm: White croaker (tomcod/kingfish) are one of the most abundant fish at SoCal and central CA piers; they eat almost anything.

species.name: Starry flounder
species.bait: Pile worms; sand shrimp; clam necks; cut anchovy
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig; spreader bar
species.lures: Small paddle-tail swimbaits, Gulp grubs on jighead
species.explanation_cold: Starry flounder move into bays and estuaries during winter and are a popular pier catch from NorCal through Washington.
species.explanation_warm: Starry flounder retreat to deeper, cooler water during summer months.

species.name: Pacific sanddab
species.bait: Clams, sand lance, squid strips, small shrimp; tiny baits on small hooks are best
species.rig: Light multi-hook bottom rig with 4-6 small dropper loops; drift over sandy bottom at 20-100 ft
species.lures: Very small jigs tipped with bait
species.explanation_cold: Pacific sanddabs are found on sandy bottom year-round at 20-300 ft; they are accessible from piers and party boats throughout the year.
species.explanation_warm: Summer and fall are the best times for sanddabs on party boats; limits of these small but delicious flatfish are common — they are considered one of California's finest eating fish.

species.name: Kelp greenling
species.bait: Shrimp; pile worms; mussels; cut squid; small crabs
species.rig: Hi-lo rig; dropper loop near bottom
species.lures: Small jigs, Gulp shrimp near kelp
species.explanation_cold: Kelp greenling hold near rocky structure year-round but bite less aggressively in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Kelp greenling are colorful bottom fish found around kelp and rocky piers from Central CA to Washington; the males have bright blue spots.

species.name: Cabezon
species.bait: Shrimp; squid; mussels; cut fish; pile worms
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig near rocks; dropper loop
species.lures: Large swimbaits and jigs near rocky structure; aggressive on large rubber baits
species.explanation_cold: Cabezon move into shallower water during fall and winter to spawn; they're one of the largest sculpin family fish on the Pacific Coast and are aggressive biters.
species.explanation_warm: Cabezon are present but in deeper water; focus on rocky jetties and deepwater piers.

species.name: Grass rockfish
species.bait: Pile worms; shrimp; cut squid; mussels
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig near rocks; hi-lo rig
species.lures: Small jigs, paddle tails near kelp and grass beds
species.explanation_cold: Grass rockfish hunker in rocky crevices during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Grass rockfish inhabit shallow rocky areas and tide pools; they are common from piers and jetties along central and northern California.

species.name: Blue rockfish
species.bait: Small pieces of squid; cut anchovy; shrimp; Sabiki rig (artificial)
species.rig: Hi-lo rig; shrimp fly rigs; small jigs
species.lures: Jigs, soft plastics near rocky structure
species.explanation_cold: Blue rockfish hold deep during winter but can be caught from deep piers.
species.explanation_warm: Blue rockfish are common around kelp beds, piers, and rocky structures in NorCal and Oregon; they school up and can be caught readily on small baits.

species.name: Copper rockfish
species.bait: Squid strips; shrimp; cut anchovy; live bait
species.rig: Hi-lo rig; dropper loop rig
species.lures: Small-medium jigs, swimbaits near rocky bottom
species.explanation_cold: Copper rockfish hold near rocky structure year-round but are less active in cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Copper rockfish are solitary ambush predators found around kelp and rocky reefs; they're accessible from deep piers and jetties.

species.name: Monkeyface prickleback
species.bait: Small crabs, mussels, tiny shrimp; found in rocky intertidal zone
species.rig: Ultra-light bottom rig in tide pools and rocky intertidal with small hook near bottom
species.lures: Very small tube jigs, micro soft plastics
species.explanation_cold: Monkeyface pricklebacks live in rocky intertidal and shallow subtidal habitat year-round along the Pacific coast.
species.explanation_warm: Spring through fall in rocky intertidal zone; a beloved target for kids and beginners fishing rocky California and Oregon coastlines — tasty and surprisingly challenging on light gear.

species.name: Striped bass (West Coast)
species.bait: Live anchovies, shad, swimbaits in San Francisco Bay and Sacramento River
species.rig: Medium to heavy spinning or conventional in bay and delta
species.lures: Swimbaits, topwater lures, trolled lures in bay and delta
species.explanation_cold: Sacramento striped bass are a non-native population introduced from the Atlantic in 1879. They established themselves as one of the most popular game fish in California, supporting a world-class fishery in San Francisco Bay and the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. Large fish (over 50 lbs) are occasionally caught. Population has declined from historical levels but remains significant.
species.explanation_warm: California striped bass minimum size is 18 inches with a 2-fish daily bag limit. Fall migration into the Delta in October-November draws large numbers of fish. San Francisco Bay striped bass are plentiful in spring when anchovies school near the bay. No commercial harvest of striped bass in California.

species.name: Chinook salmon
species.bait: Whole or plug-cut herring trolled with flasher; anchovies; sand lance; cured roe near river mouths in fall
species.rig: Mooching rig with 2-hook herring setup; downrigger trolling with flasher-herring at 40-120 ft
species.sinker: 4-12 oz mooching sinker; downrigger ball to depth
species.lures: Spoons (Coho Killer, Coyote, Apex), hoochies on 36-in leader behind flasher, spinners near river mouths
species.explanation_cold: Fall and winter Chinook (blackmouth) school nearshore in Puget Sound and coastal bays; they feed near the bottom in 60-200 ft and are targeted on downriggers with herring.
species.explanation_warm: Spring ocean Chinook feed aggressively on herring and anchovies; trolling cut-plug herring with a 4-6 oz mooching sinker near bait balls at 40-80 ft produces the most fish.

species.name: Coho salmon
species.bait: Whole herring, anchovies, sand lance; pink shrimp; cured salmon eggs near estuaries in fall
species.rig: Trolling with flasher and 36-inch leader; mooching rig with whole herring; surface trolling in summer
species.sinker: 2-6 oz mooching weight or no weight at surface
species.lures: Spoons (Krocodile, Coyote), hoochies in pink/chartreuse/white, buzz bombs, Stingsilda jigs; Clousers on fly
species.explanation_cold: Coho stage in estuaries and near river mouths in fall before their spawning run; they feed heavily and are accessible from river-mouth jetties and near-shore structure.
species.explanation_warm: Summer coho feed aggressively near the surface and upper water column; surface trolling with flasher-hoochie at 20-60 ft is standard, and fish will smash spoons and jigs near bait schools.

species.name: Leopard shark
species.bait: Squid; cut mackerel; anchovy; shrimp; sand crabs
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig with wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader
species.lures: Primarily bait-caught; large soft plastic swimbaits near bottom
species.explanation_cold: Leopard sharks are in deeper water and less active during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Leopard sharks cruise shallow bays and surf zones in summer; La Jolla and Pacifica are famous spots. They are beautiful, spotted sharks and fight well.

species.name: Bat ray
species.bait: Squid; shrimp; cut mackerel; ghost shrimp; mussels
species.rig: Heavy sliding sinker rig with wire leader
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Bat rays are in deeper water and less accessible during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Bat rays are powerful fighters caught from piers and surf in California bays; they can exceed 100 lbs and will test your tackle.

species.name: Pacific mackerel
species.bait: Small pieces of cut squid; Sabiki rigs; small chrome jigs; cut anchovy
species.rig: Sabiki rig; small metal jig on light line
species.lures: Metal spoons, small jigs; caught on sabiki rigs or small fast-retrieved lures
species.explanation_cold: Pacific mackerel move offshore during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Pacific mackerel run in large schools around piers and harbors in SoCal; they're fun to catch on Sabiki rigs and make excellent live bait for larger fish.

species.name: Spotfin croaker
species.bait: Sand crabs; mussels; bloodworms; ghost shrimp
species.rig: Carolina rig; sliding sinker rig
species.lures: Small paddle-tail swimbaits, tube jigs in the surf
species.explanation_cold: Spotfin croaker move to deeper bays and offshore during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Spotfin croaker feed in the SoCal surf zone; their distinctive high-pitched croaking and golden body make them easy to identify.

species.name: Kelp bass (calico bass)
species.bait: Live anchovy; cut squid; swimbaits; artificial grubs
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig near kelp; jig head with swimbait
species.sinker: 1-2 oz sliding sinker or jig head
species.lures: Swimbaits, topwater poppers, rubber worms near kelp; voracious lure fish
species.explanation_cold: Kelp bass are less active in cold water and hold tight to structure.
species.explanation_warm: Kelp bass are the most popular gamefish from SoCal piers and jetties; they ambush baitfish around kelp beds and rocky structure.

species.name: Barred sand bass
species.bait: Live anchovy; cut squid; swimbaits; Carolina-rigged plastics
species.rig: Dropper loop rig; jig head; Carolina rig with swimbait
species.lures: Swimbaits, drop-shot rigs with small plastics; excellent jig target
species.explanation_cold: Sand bass move to deeper water during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Sand bass school over sandy bottoms and around structure in SoCal; they aggregate in large spawning groups in summer.

species.name: Spotted sand bass
species.bait: Live anchovies or small baitfish, squid strips near sandy/muddy bottom in bays
species.rig: Light to medium bottom rig in bays and nearshore areas at 10-60 ft
species.lures: Soft plastic swimbaits, small paddle-tails on light jig heads near bottom
species.explanation_cold: Spotted sand bass are bay and estuary residents in Southern California; they overlap with barred sand bass but prefer softer bottom habitat.
species.explanation_warm: Summer and fall in San Diego Bay and other Southern California coastal bays; sometimes referred to as 'bay bass' and a fun light-tackle target from kayaks and small boats.

species.name: California sheephead
species.bait: Mussels; shrimp; sea urchin; cut squid; crab
species.rig: Dropper loop rig near rocks; hi-lo rig
species.lures: Heavy jigs, swimbaits near rocky structure
species.explanation_cold: California sheephead are less active and in deeper water during winter.
species.explanation_warm: California sheephead are colorful, hard-fighting wrasse found around rocky reefs and kelp; they have powerful jaws that crush shellfish.

species.name: Opaleye
species.bait: Frozen peas; moss; mussels; small pieces of shrimp
species.rig: Float rig with small hook; light hi-lo rig
species.sinker: Split shot or small egg sinker
species.lures: Small jigs, Gulp shrimp near kelp; not a strong lure target
species.explanation_cold: Opaleye are less active but still present near rocky shorelines in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Opaleye are herbivorous fish found around rocky shorelines and jetties in SoCal; they're surprisingly hard fighters for their size.

species.name: Halfmoon
species.bait: Mussels; frozen peas; moss; small pieces of shrimp
species.rig: Float rig; light hi-lo rig
species.lures: Small jigs and soft plastics near structure
species.explanation_cold: Halfmoon hold near rocky structure during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Halfmoon are found along SoCal rocky shores and kelp beds; they're similar to opaleye and share the same habitat.

species.name: Jack mackerel
species.bait: Sabiki rigs; small jigs; cut squid; cut anchovy
species.rig: Sabiki rig or light jig setup
species.lures: Small jigs, metal spoons; same as Pacific mackerel
species.explanation_cold: Jack mackerel are offshore and not typically available from piers in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Jack mackerel school around SoCal piers in summer and fall; they are aggressive feeders and excellent for bait or eating.

species.name: Pacific barracuda
species.bait: Live anchovies; small mackerel; chrome surface iron jigs; white swimbaits
species.rig: Light to medium spinning or casting rod; wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader (single strand wire preferred)
species.sinker: None for surface jigs; split shot for live bait
species.lures: Long tube lures, Rapala plugs, large needlefish-style jigs; fast retrieve
species.explanation_cold: Pacific barracuda move south into Mexican waters or offshore when temperatures drop below 60°F; catches are uncommon in Southern California from December through February.
species.explanation_warm: Pacific barracuda school near kelp paddies, the surface, and nearshore reefs from San Diego to Point Conception; they hit chrome surface iron jigs and live anchovies aggressively on light tackle from boats and piers.

species.name: Pacific bonito
species.bait: Live anchovy; Sabiki-caught bait; metal jigs; feathered lures
species.rig: Live bait on sliding sinker; casting jig; trolling feather
species.lures: Metal spoons, fast jigs, feather lures; excellent topwater action when schooling
species.explanation_cold: Pacific bonito are offshore during cool months.
species.explanation_warm: Pacific bonito (a small tuna relative) chase baitfish schools past SoCal piers; they fight hard and are great on light tackle.

species.name: Yellowtail
species.bait: Live sardine; live mackerel; iron jigs; surface poppers
species.rig: Live bait on heavy fluorocarbon leader; yo-yo iron jig
species.sinker: None (free-lined live bait) or 1-2 oz sliding sinker
species.lures: Swimbaits (6-9" kite-fish style), iron jigs (flylined), Yo-Zuri/Rapala plugs; premier lure target
species.explanation_cold: Yellowtail migrate south to Baja during cold months.
species.explanation_warm: Yellowtail cruise past SoCal piers and kelp beds chasing baitfish; these are powerful fighters and one of the most prized pier catches on the West Coast.

species.name: Queenfish
species.bait: Anchovies, sardines near the surface in Southern California bays and nearshore
species.rig: Light spinning near surface schools in bays
species.lures: Small spoons and jigs near surface schools
species.explanation_cold: Queenfish are an abundant summer species in Southern California bays; they school near the surface and hit lures eagerly.
species.explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Southern California bays; form large surface schools — a fast-action light-tackle species.

species.name: Sargo
species.bait: Mussels, clams, shrimp near rocky reef and kelp at 5-60 ft in Southern California
species.rig: Light rig near rocky reef and kelp
species.lures: Small grubs near rocky bottom
species.explanation_cold: Sargo are found on rocky reef and kelp in Southern California; they feed on invertebrates near rocky structure.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round on Southern California rocky reef; common around rocky jetties and kelp beds — good panfish.

species.name: Shovelnose guitarfish
species.bait: Sand crabs; squid; cut fish; shrimp; bloodworms
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig; Carolina rig
species.lures: Not typically targeted with lures
species.explanation_cold: Shovelnose guitarfish are in deeper water during winter.
species.explanation_warm: Shovelnose guitarfish are common in SoCal surf and bays; these ray-shark hybrids root through sand for crabs and worms.

species.name: Round stingray
species.bait: Ghost shrimp, sand crabs, mussels, clam strips, bloodworms; ghost shrimp are the primary bait in Southern California surf
species.rig: Carolina rig or fish finder rig; rays lie motionless on sandy bottom — keep bait stationary on the sand
species.explanation_cold: Round stingrays move to deeper water in winter and are largely absent from the nearshore surf zone below 58°F.
species.explanation_warm: Round stingrays are abundant in Southern California surf zones from late spring through fall; they feed on ghost shrimp and worms buried in the sand. Catch and release recommended.

species.name: Omilu (bluefin trevally)
species.bait: Live baitfish; cut squid; poppers; metal jigs
species.rig: Sliding sinker rig; popping/spinning setup; papio rig
species.lures: Poppers, jigs, stickbaits; aggressive lure fish
species.explanation_cold: Bluefin trevally are present year-round but slightly less active in winter.
species.explanation_warm: Bluefin trevally (omilu) are strikingly beautiful blue-finned jacks found around reefs and rocky shores in Hawaii; they hit lures and bait aggressively.

species.name: Menpachi
species.bait: Small shrimp; cut squid; aku belly (skipjack tuna belly); bread
species.rig: Small hook dropper rig; float rig near rocks
species.sinker: Split shot or small bank sinker
species.lures: Small jigs near structure at night
species.explanation_cold: Menpachi are active year-round in Hawaii, feeding at night around rocky areas.
species.explanation_warm: Menpachi (soldierfish/squirrelfish) are a prized eating fish in Hawaii; they come out at night to feed around rocks and reef edges near piers.

species.name: Aholehole
species.bait: Bread; small shrimp; dough balls; bread flies; palu (chum)
species.rig: Float rig with small hook; light bottom rig
species.lures: Small jigs near structure
species.explanation_cold: Aholehole are active year-round in Hawaii harbors and rocky shorelines.
species.explanation_warm: Aholehole are one of Hawaii's most popular panfish; they school around piers, harbors, and river mouths and are great eating.

species.name: Weke (goatfish)
species.bait: Small shrimp; pieces of squid; cut fish; sandworms
species.rig: Light bottom rig with small hook; two-hook bottom rig in sandy areas
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near sandy bottom
species.explanation_cold: Weke are year-round Hawaii residents; they forage along sandy bottoms and reef edges using their chin barbels to detect buried invertebrates.
species.explanation_warm: Weke (goatfish) are a beloved Hawaiian table fish found in schools over sandy flats, grass beds, and mixed reef-sand edges; they are excellent eating and bite readily on small baits fished on the bottom.

species.name: Akule
species.bait: Sabiki rigs with small hooks; also caught by cast net
species.rig: Sabiki rig fished near the surface or mid-water in Hawaiian harbors and bays
species.lures: Tiny metal jigs in silver; primarily a sabiki rig target
species.explanation_cold: Akule school year-round in Hawaiian harbors and nearshore waters; large schools are visible at the surface at dawn.
species.explanation_warm: Spring through fall produces the largest schools of akule nearshore; prized as live bait for ulua and other large predators, and excellent eating when salted and dried (traditionally).

species.name: Opelu
species.bait: Sabiki rigs; very small hooks with minimal bait; also cast-netted in large numbers
species.rig: Sabiki rig fished mid-water to 60 ft in Hawaiian coastal waters
species.lures: Tiny silver jigs, sabiki rigs
species.explanation_cold: Opelu school around Hawaiian harbors, bays, and nearshore seamounts year-round.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round target for live bait; opelu are Hawaii's premier live bait for ahi and other big game — a cast-net full of live opelu is worth its weight in gold on a big-game trip.

species.name: Ta'ape
species.bait: Small shrimp, squid strips, tiny pieces of fish near reef structure
species.rig: Light bottom rig near shallow reef at 10-60 ft; small hooks required
species.lures: Small jigs in yellow/blue, tiny soft plastic grubs near reef
species.explanation_cold: Taape (introduced from French Polynesia) are year-round residents on Hawaiian shallow reefs, often forming large schools.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round abundant species on Hawaiian reefs; easy to catch and good eating — they are an introduced species and there are no bag limits, so harvest is encouraged.

species.name: To'au
species.bait: Cut squid; small fish chunks; shrimp; live small fish
species.rig: Bottom rig with light to medium sinker; slip sinker rig near reef structure
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near reef structure
species.explanation_cold: Toau are active year-round around Hawaii's shallow reef flats and rocky shorelines; water temperature in Hawaii rarely limits the bite.
species.explanation_warm: Toau (blacktail snapper) are one of Hawaii's most common and easily caught shore fish; they congregate around reef structure, rocky points, and reef edges — great eating and fun on light tackle.

species.name: Uku
species.bait: Live baitfish (small akule, nehu), fresh squid, or cut fish near mid-depth reefs
species.rig: Live bait rig with 40-60 lb fluorocarbon leader; light to medium bottom rig at 100-300 ft
species.lures: Vertical jigs in blue/silver/white (100-200g), soft plastic swimbaits, live bait on light gear
species.explanation_cold: Uku hold near mid-depth reefs and bottom structure at 100-400 ft year-round and are accessible throughout winter.
species.explanation_warm: Spring and summer are peak uku season in Hawaii; they school near rocky bottom and pinnacles and hit jigs and live bait aggressively — one of Hawaii's most popular nearshore targets.

species.name: Kaku (barracuda)
species.bait: Live baitfish; cut fish strips; silver spoons; jigs
species.rig: Wire leader with live bait; casting spoon or jig
species.sinker: None (cast and retrieve) or 1-2 oz sliding sinker
species.lures: Long tube lures, needlefish-style jigs, large silver spoons; fast retrieve
species.explanation_cold: Kaku are present year-round in Hawaii harbors and reefs.
species.explanation_warm: Kaku (great barracuda) patrol Hawaii harbors, piers, and reef edges; they strike fast and fight hard on light tackle.

species.name: Nenue
species.bait: Sea lettuce and other algae (natural food); bread balls, cooked rice, or dough bait work best
species.rig: Ultra-light float rig with tiny hooks and dough bait or algae; light 8-12 lb line
species.lures: Not a lure target; requires natural or dough bait presentations
species.explanation_cold: Nenue (chub) are resident on shallow Hawaiian reefs and surge zones year-round.
species.explanation_warm: Summer is peak nenue fishing around Hawaiian pier pilings, rocky shores, and shallow reef areas; they respond to bread and dough bait and are a fun light-tackle species.

species.name: Kala
species.bait: Limu (seaweed), bread bait, or tiny invertebrate pieces near reef edges
species.rig: Ultra-light float or bottom rig with very small hook; light 10-15 lb line
species.lures: Not a lure target; requires plant-based or dough bait
species.explanation_cold: Kala (bluespine unicornfish) are resident on Hawaiian reefs year-round, grazing on algae along reef edges and surge zones.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round target on Hawaiian reefs; most active in warmer months near surge channels and reef edges where algae grows abundantly — a light-tackle challenge on small hooks.

species.name: Manini
species.bait: Limu (algae), bread balls, cooked noodles, or rice compressed on a tiny hook
species.rig: Ultra-light float rig with size 8-12 hook; 6-10 lb line; fish in tide pools and shallow reef
species.lures: Not a lure species; requires plant-based bait
species.explanation_cold: Manini are schooling surgeonfish resident on shallow Hawaiian reefs year-round.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round shallow-water target in Hawaii; often seen in large schools over rocky reef and tide pools — challenging to hook due to small mouth but a traditional Hawaiian subsistence fish.

species.name: Uhu (parrotfish)
species.bait: Small crab pieces, sea urchin, bread bait near coral reef; they scrape algae from coral
species.rig: Light to medium bottom rig near coral and reef structure
species.lures: Not commonly caught on lures; small jigs near reef occasionally work
species.explanation_cold: Uhu are reef-dwelling parrotfish present year-round on Hawaiian coral reefs.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round target near Hawaiian coral reefs; uhu are highly prized as food fish and were a traditional Hawaiian delicacy — they are regulated and most anglers practice selective harvest.

species.name: Ama'ama (mullet)
species.bait: Algae, dough bait, micro-bread balls near shallow sandy flats and estuaries; cast net is most effective
species.rig: Cast net in shallow estuaries and fishponds; light float rig with bread bait
species.lures: Not typically a lure target
species.explanation_cold: Amaama (striped mullet) are year-round in Hawaiian coastal waters and fishponds; they run in schools that are traditionally netted.
species.explanation_warm: Year-round but best in cooler months; amaama are deeply embedded in Hawaiian cultural fishing history — traditionally harvested with throw nets in coastal fishponds. They are excellent eating.

species.name: Mu
species.bait: Shrimp; squid; small crabs; cut fish
species.rig: Bottom rig with fluorocarbon leader; dropper loop
species.lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near bottom structure
species.explanation_cold: Mu are present year-round around reef structure but less active in cooler months.
species.explanation_warm: Mu (bigeye emperor) are prized bottom fish in Hawaii caught from rocky shores and piers over reef; they are excellent eating.

species.name: Roi
species.bait: Live small fish; cut fish; squid strips; lures near structure
species.rig: Bottom rig near reef structure; small jig or drop-shot rig around rocky habitat
species.lures: Jigs, swimbaits near reef
species.explanation_cold: Roi are active year-round in Hawaii; this invasive grouper occupies reef habitat year-round and can be caught on most bottom rigs near structure.
species.explanation_warm: Roi (peacock grouper) are an invasive species in Hawaii introduced in the 1950s; they are abundant on coral reefs, rocky bottoms, and rubble zones — anglers are encouraged to keep all they catch as part of control efforts.
